title: What do the NDIS incident management rules require, and must workers be trained on them?
description: NDIS Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules 2018: system procedures, the section 13 training duty, 24 hour and 5 day notices and 7 year records.
shortAnswer: Yes. Every registered NDIS provider must run a documented incident management system that complies with the NDIS (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018, and section 13 requires that system to include training for everyone the provider employs or engages in using and complying with it. Workers must tell a manager or key personnel about a reportable incident as soon as possible; the provider must notify the NDIS Commission within 24 hours or 5 business days depending on the incident.
keyTakeaways: Section 13(3) of the Incident Management Rules makes worker training on the incident management system a mandatory part of that system for registered providers.
Section 19 puts a personal duty on each worker to notify key personnel, a supervisor or manager, or the nominated reporting person as soon as possible after becoming aware of a reportable incident.

Death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or assault, and sexual misconduct must be notified within 24 hours; other reportable incidents, mainly unauthorized restrictive practices, within 5 business days.
Incident records and reportable incident records must be kept for 7 years, and the Commissioner can require a final report within 60 business days.
Since October 12, 2026, new reportable incidents are lodged in the new NDIS Commission Portal.
appliesTo: Registered NDIS providers, through section 73Y of the NDIS Act
Every person employed or otherwise engaged by a registered provider
Key personnel and the person nominated to report incidents to the NDIS Commission
Unregistered providers, as guidance only (the Code of Conduct still requires them to respond to incidents)

sections.heading: What do the NDIS Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules require?

blocks.text: They require each registered provider to implement and maintain an incident management system, and to notify and manage reportable incidents. Section 73Y of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 imposes the system duty, which must be appropriate to the provider's size and the classes of supports it delivers, and non-compliance is a breach of a condition of registration. The detail sits in the [National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2018L00633/latest/text) (the Incident Management Rules), which the Federal Register of Legislation shows as the as made version of May 18, 2018. This page states the position as at November 2026.

Section 9 defines what the system must cover: acts, omissions, events or circumstances connected with supports that have, or could have, caused harm to a person with disability; acts by a person with disability that caused serious harm or risk of serious harm to another person; and alleged reportable incidents. That scope is wider than reportable incidents, so a provider's training cannot stop at the list of reportable incident types.

The NDIS Practice Standards reinforce the rules. The core module's incident management outcome includes the indicator "All workers are aware of, trained in, and comply with the required procedures in relation to incident management", and both the core and verification modules require a system that complies with the rules ([core module](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/ndis-practice-standards/core-module-provider-governance-and-operational)). Other training indicators are covered in [what training NDIS workers need](/regulations/ndis-practice-standards-worker-training).

sections.heading: Is incident management training mandatory for NDIS workers?

blocks.text: Yes, for registered providers. Section 13 of the Incident Management Rules, headed 'Roles, responsibilities, compliance and training of workers', sets three requirements for the system:

items: it must set out the roles and responsibilities of every person employed or otherwise engaged by the provider in identifying, managing and resolving incidents and in preventing them (section 13(1));
it must provide that each such person must comply with the system (section 13(2)); and

it "must include requirements relating to the provision of training to any persons employed or otherwise engaged by the registered NDIS provider in the use of, and compliance with, the incident management system" (section 13(3)).

blocks.text: Section 12 adds an awareness duty: the provider must give a copy of the documented system, in an accessible form, to each person it employs or engages, and assist them to understand how it operates. Together, sections 12 and 13 mean a provider must be able to show who is covered, what each role must do, and that each person was trained. The rules do not set hours or a refresher interval; the provider sets those in its own training requirements. The term 'employed or otherwise engaged' reaches contractors and volunteers as well as employees.

For unregistered providers the position is guidance. The NDIS Commission says all NDIS providers should have an incident management system, and that the Code of Conduct requires all providers to respond to incidents ([incident management](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/reportable-incidents-and-incident-management/incident-management)). See [NDIS Code of Conduct and worker orientation](/regulations/ndis-code-of-conduct-and-worker-orientation).

sections.heading: What must the incident management system's procedures cover?

blocks.text: Section 10 requires procedures for identifying, managing and resolving incidents, and each procedure is a candidate learning outcome. The procedures must specify how incidents are identified, recorded and reported; to whom they are reported; who reports reportable incidents to the Commissioner; how affected people with disability are supported, including access to independent advocates; how they are involved in resolution; when an investigation is needed; and when corrective action is required.

Every incident must be assessed for whether it could have been prevented, how well it was managed, what remedial action is needed, and who else must be told, considering the views of the people affected (section 10(3)). The system must provide for periodic review of its effectiveness (section 10(6)) and must afford procedural fairness when an incident is dealt with (section 11), which matters when the incident concerns a worker's conduct.

Section 12(2) lists twelve minimum details for each incident record, including a description and the harm caused, whether it is reportable, time and place, people and witnesses involved, the assessment, actions taken, consultation with affected people, any investigation and its outcome, and who made the record. Records must be kept for 7 years. The NDIS Commission's case study of a worker who noticed unexplained bruising shows the intended chain: the worker reported straight away under a known procedure, the provider notified the Commission within 24 hours, and the review led to improved staff training in recognizing signs of possible abuse or injury.

sections.heading: Which incidents must be reported to the NDIS Commission, and how fast?

blocks.text: Reportable incidents are defined in section 73Z(4) of the NDIS Act and adjusted by section 16 of the rules. Timeframes run from when the provider became aware of the incident, and alleged incidents count as if they had occurred (section 17). The NDIS Commission's [reportable incidents page](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/reportable-incidents-and-incident-management/reportable-incidents) summarizes them as follows.

blocks.text: For 24 hour incidents, if full information is not available in time, the provider gives core details within 24 hours and the rest within 5 business days, and must add witness details and proposed further actions within 5 business days (section 20). The Commission notes that an incident resulting in harm must be reported within 24 hours, and that late reporting may lead to an infringement notice. The provider must update the Commissioner on significant new information (section 23), and the Commissioner may require a final report on any investigation within 60 business days (section 24). Restrictive practice incidents are explained in [NDIS restrictive practices and behavior support rules](/regulations/ndis-restrictive-practices-and-behaviour-support-training).

blocks.title: New portal from October 12, 2026
blocks.text: The NDIS Commission states that all new incidents, including the 24 hour and 5 day reports, are lodged in the new NDIS Commission Portal from October 12, 2026. Incidents lodged before that date stay in the existing portal for 5 day reports, requests for information and weekly unauthorized restrictive practice reporting. Staff instructions and job aids should name the correct portal for each case.

sections.heading: What must individual workers and key personnel do?

blocks.text: Workers have a direct duty under section 19: a person employed or otherwise engaged by a registered provider who becomes aware of a reportable incident must notify, as soon as possible, a member of key personnel, their supervisor or manager, or the person nominated to report incidents to the Commissioner. Key personnel and the nominated reporting person must take all reasonable steps to ensure reportable incidents are notified to the Commissioner (section 18).

This gives each role a distinct learning outcome. A support worker needs to recognize the six categories, including allegations and indirect indicators such as a change in behavior, and know the internal route. A supervisor needs to judge the 24 hour or 5 day category and escalate. The nominated reporting person needs to complete the portal notification and know what section 22 lets them withhold, for example where obtaining information could prejudice a criminal investigation or expose a person with disability to harm.

blocks.text: The last row closes the loop: section 12(5) requires the system to collect statistics to identify systemic issues, and the core module expects incident review to feed improvement. Where reviews show a pattern, updated training is the documented response, as the Commission's own case study illustrates. Incident reviews also trigger a review of any [worker screening risk management plan](/regulations/ndis-worker-screening-requirements) under the Worker Screening Rules. For the sector context, see [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each section of the Incident Management Rules to role specific learning outcomes and assessment points, so a support worker, supervisor and nominated reporting person are each assessed on their own duty. When incident reviews identify a gap, the affected outcomes and roles are visible, which is the evidence of improvement section 10(6) and the core module look for.

faqs.q: Does the verification module require incident management training?
faqs.a: The verification module's incident management indicator requires a system that complies with the Incident Management Rules. Because section 13(3) of those rules requires the system to include training requirements for everyone employed or engaged, providers audited under the verification module still need incident management training, even though the explicit 'trained in' indicator appears in the core module.

faqs.q: Who is the nominated reporting person under the NDIS incident rules?
faqs.a: Section 10(1)(c) requires the incident management system to specify the person responsible for reporting reportable incidents to the Commissioner. That person, together with key personnel, must take all reasonable steps to ensure notifications are made, and workers can notify them directly under section 19.

faqs.q: Do alleged incidents have to be reported to the NDIS Commission?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 17 of the Incident Management Rules says a reference to a reportable incident that has occurred includes one that is alleged to have occurred. Providers must notify within the same 24 hour or 5 business day timeframes and record the allegation under section 12(3).

faqs.q: How long must NDIS incident records be kept?
faqs.a: Seven years. Section 12(4) applies to records of incidents and alleged reportable incidents from the day the record is made, and section 25 applies to reportable incident records from the day notification was given to the Commissioner. Other Commonwealth, state or territory record retention laws may also apply.
